overview.body:
**Sbk** ​(*sobek*) — ‌The Nile, ‌Fertility, Military ​Power · ​He who ​causes ​to be ​fertile — ‌belongs to ​the Egyptian ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Nile, ‌Fertility, Crocodiles". ​The name ​means "He ​who ​causes to ​be fertile ‌(Egyptian sbk)"[^1].

​**Sbk** — ‌Sobek — ​is ‌the crocodile ​god of ‌the Nile’s ​dangerous fertility: ‌the animal ​that ​kills at ‌the water’s ‌edge and ‌the power ​that makes ​the flood ‌bring ​life. In ​the Middle ‌Kingdom he ​rose from ​local river ‌god ​to a ‌creator deity ​in his ​own right, ​and his ​cult ‌centres — ‌Crocodilopolis and ​Kom Ombo ‌— kept ​living sacred ​crocodiles as ‌his ‌incarnations.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ‌name as ​**Sbk** and ‌serves its ​temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/sobek/). The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *sobek* ​survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by ​the early ‌domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ​not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Hieroglyphs ​as ​**𓃣**. ​Etymologically it ​means ‌"He ​who ​causes to ‌be ​fertile ‌(Egyptian ​sbk)"[^1].

The ‌ASCII ​form ​*sobek* ​survives ​only because ​the ‌early ​domain-name ‌system could ​not ‌carry ​diacritics; ‌it ​is a ‌technological ​compromise, ​not ‌an ancient ‌spelling. ‌The ​Unicode ​restoration **Sbk** ‌recovers ​the ​full ‌diacritic ​detail of ​the ‌scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly in ​the ​address ​bar. ​The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ‌form ​— ‌a ​description computed ​from ‌the ‌displayed ‌form itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- ​**s** → ​**S** ‌— ​Same
- ​**o** → ​**—** ‌— ​Dropped: ​vowel ​not written
- ‌**b** ​→ ‌**b** ​— Same
- ‌**e** ​→ ‌**—** ‌— Dropped: ​vowel ​not ​written
- ​**k** ‌→ **k** ‌— ​Same

sources.citation: James P. Allen, Middle Egyptian: An Introduction to the Language and Culture of Hieroglyphs, Cambridge University Press, 2000.
Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian.

domains.body:
**Sbk** ​— Sobek ‌— is ‌the ​crocodile god ​of ​the Nile’s ​dangerous fertility: ​the ‌animal that ​kills ​at the ‌water’s edge ​and ‌the power ​that ‌makes the ​flood bring ​life. ​In the ​Middle ​Kingdom he ‌rose from ​local ‌river god ​to ‌a creator ​deity in ‌his ​own right, ‌and ​his cult ​centres — ‌Crocodilopolis ‌and Kom ‌Ombo ​— kept ​living sacred ‌crocodiles ​as his ​incarnations.[^1]

### ‌Lord of ​the Waters

​Master ‌of the ​Nile ‌and its ​inundation; the ​flood ​itself was ​called ‌“the arrival ‌of Sobek”.

### ​The ‌Crocodile God

​Incarnate ​in Crocodylus ‌niloticus; temple ‌pools ‌held living ‌sacred ​crocodiles adorned ‌with jewellery.

### ​Creator ​and Solar ​Eye

‌In Middle ​Kingdom theology ​he ​emerges from ‌the ​primordial waters; ​at Kom ​Ombo ‌he shares ​a ‌temple with ​Horus.

### Patron ‌of ​the Army

‌Soldiers ‌and the ​Pharaoh’s power; ​his ​epithets link ​him ‌to strength ‌and military ​might.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Sbk concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, each ‌a ​compressed ‌statement ​about ‌the ​name:[^1]

- ​**Lord of ​the ​Waters** ​— ‌Master ​of ‌the ​Nile ‌and its ​inundation; ‌the ​flood ‌itself ​was ​called ‌“the arrival ‌of ‌Sobek”.
- ​**The ​Crocodile ‌God** ​— ​Incarnate in ‌Crocodylus ​niloticus; ​temple ‌pools ​held ‌living ​sacred ​crocodiles adorned ​with ​jewellery.
- ‌**Creator ‌and ​Solar ‌Eye** ​— In ​Middle ‌Kingdom ‌theology ‌he ‌emerges ​from ‌the primordial ​waters; ​at ​Kom ‌Ombo ​he ​shares ​a ‌temple with ​Horus.
- ​**Patron ​of ‌the ​Army** ‌— ​Soldiers and ‌the ​Pharaoh’s ‌power; ‌his ​epithets ​link ​him to ​strength ‌and ‌military ​might.

mythology.body:
Sobek has ​no single continuous myth-cycle; ‌his theology was ‌assembled from the ​river itself — the ​annual flood that ​could drown or feed ​— and from ​the pharaonic appetite ‌for a god who ​united raw natural ​violence with legitimate ‌kingship. The Middle Kingdom ​elevated him to ‌cosmic rank: a creator ​who rises from ‌the Nun, the ​primordial water.[^1]

### The Crocodile ​Who Emerges from ​Nun (Fayum Theology)

The ​Sobek theology of ​the Fayum — ‌best preserved in the ​hymn cycles of ‌the crocodile temples ​— casts him as ‌the one who ​first climbed from the ‌primeval waters, creator ​of the world’s ‌order and of the ​Nile itself. Later ​tradition even made him ‌a form of ‌the sun god’s ‌power, the fierce Eye ​of Ra returned ​from the Nubian ‌desert.[^2]

### The Double Temple ​(Kom Ombo)

At ​Kom Ombo south of ‌Luxor, Sobek shares ​a perfectly symmetrical ​double temple with Horus ‌the Elder: one ​half for the falcon ‌of the sky, ​one for the ​crocodile of the river. ​The division stages ​the Egyptian ideal of ‌the Two Lands’ ‌balance — sky ​and water, kingship and ‌fertility — under ​one roof.

### Sobek ​and the Wonders at ‌Court (Papyrus Westcar)

‌In the Westcar Papyrus’ ‌cycle of Khufu-era ‌wonders, the crocodile ​motif appears in the ‌tale of the ​adulterer punished by a ​wax crocodile that ​comes alive at ‌a word — a ​demonstration that the ​river-god’s animal is ​an instrument of moral ‌order, released and ​recalled by priestly power.

### ​Petsuchos, the Sacred ​Crocodile (Greek Reportage)

‌Strabo and Herodotus describe ​the living god ‌of Crocodilopolis: a great ​crocodile called *Petsuchos*, ‌kept in a ​pool, fed by priests, ‌adorned with gold ‌and crystal rings. ​When it died the ​city mourned; a ​new Petsuchos was sought ​among the river ‌animals by oracular ‌selection — the god ​re-incarnating indefinitely.
